title: Designing a permission system

facts.text: An access control list (ACL) is a list of rules that specifies which users are granted or denied access to a particular resource.
ACL is easy to understand, but it is error-prone and its maintenance cost is high.
Discretionary access control (DAC) is based on ACL: it grants or restricts object access through an access policy determined by the object's owner group.
DAC is easy and flexible, and the Linux file system supports it, but permission control is scattered and the object's owner group has too much power.
In mandatory access control (MAC) both resource owners and resources have classification labels, and different labels are granted different permissions.
MAC is strict and straightforward, but not flexible.
Attribute-based access control (ABAC) evaluates permissions based on attributes of the resource owner, the action, the resource and the environment.
ABAC is flexible, but its rules can be complicated and the implementation is hard; it is not commonly used.
Role-based access control (RBAC) evaluates permissions based on roles, and is flexible in assigning roles.

notes: thin: the guide only lists five access-control models with pros and cons; no requirements, scale, data model, API, policy engine, or advice on which model to choose.

definition.text: A list of rules that specifies which users are granted or denied access to a particular resource.

facts.text: An ACL is a list of rules that specifies which users are granted or denied access to a particular resource.
An access policy can be expressed as an access control list.
ACLs are easy to understand, but they are error-prone and their maintenance cost is high.

Even when access is controlled by authentication plus access control lists, maintaining the authorization data is not trivial and often costs as much administration as managing authentication credentials.

definition.text: An access-control model, built on ACLs, in which an access policy determined by the object's owner group grants or restricts access to the object.

facts.text: DAC is based on ACL and grants or restricts object access through an access policy determined by the object's owner group.
DAC is easy and flexible, and the Linux file system supports it.
Its drawbacks are scattered permission control and too much power for the object's owner group.

definition.text: An access-control model in which resource owners and resources carry classification labels, and each label is granted its own permissions.

facts.text: In MAC both resource owners and resources have classification labels, and different labels are granted different permissions.
MAC is strict and straightforward.
MAC is not flexible.

definition.text: An access-control model that evaluates permissions from attributes of the resource owner, the action, the resource and the environment.

facts.text: ABAC evaluates permissions based on attributes of the resource owner, the action, the resource and the environment.
ABAC is flexible.
Its rules can be complicated and the implementation is hard, so it is not commonly used.

definition.text: An access-control model that evaluates permissions from the roles a subject has been granted.

facts.text: RBAC evaluates permissions based on roles: subjects are granted one or more roles, and the resource being accessed is checked for having been assigned at least one of those roles. It is a widely used model in modern systems.
RBAC is flexible in assigning roles.
In Kubernetes' RBAC mode, access rights are granted to users based on the roles granted to them, and each role defines a list of allowed actions.
